articles.title: REP BRIAN MAST: We are protecting our troops from having our own tech used against them
articles.summary: Trump's proposed rules target American investments flowing to the Chinese Communist Party's military-industrial base in AI and semiconductors.
articles.body: The key objective in economic warfare is to do more harm to your enemy than you do to yourself, and President Donald Trump is doing what every American president should do: putting America first and making sure the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) cannot use our own resources against us. Let’s be clear about what we are dealing with. The CCP is not our friend. It is a strategic adversary that wants to weaken the United States, challenge our military and place itself in leadership around the world. China is pouring resources into the technologies that will define the next generation of warfare. It wants more advanced weapons, better targeting systems, stronger cyber capabilities and every technological advantage it can get its hands on. And you better believe they will buy, cheat and steal their way to getting it, so in no way should we, the United States of America, be helping them get there faster. For too long, American capital and expertise have found their way into Chinese companies developing technologies with military applications. And for anyone to argue that every part of China’s economy isn’t linked directly to the CCP military clearly hasn’t been paying attention. That is a serious national security failure. We should never allow our investments, our ingenuity or our world-class research to give the CCP an advantage over the United States. TRUMP'S QUIET CHINA WINS ARE MORE IMPORTANT THAN XI'S EMPTY STATE VISIT That’s why I couldn’t be happier to see the Trump administration propose new rules to put an end to Chinese infiltration. By strengthening restrictions on investments that could help build China's military-industrial base, the administration is taking meaningful action to protect the technologies that keep America strong. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the administration deserve a huge amount of credit for advancing these protections and working to ensure that American money does not end up strengthening our greatest foreign adversary. The COINS Act was a great step forward to provide a stronger foundation for preventing American investment from supporting sensitive technologies in countries that threaten our national security. Now, we are making sure those protections have teeth. CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE We are closing loopholes, addressing the ways financial and professional services can help Chinese companies advance, and ensuring that restrictions keep pace with the technologies Beijing is trying to acquire. Because this is not just about money. It is about American lives. I served in the Army. I know what it means to put on a uniform and accept the responsibility of defending this country. To pray that our military is better and stronger than our enemy’s. But our service members don’t get to choose whether the enemy they face has better technology. And we should never ask them to confront an adversary that we helped make stronger. BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN Think about the consequences. Every technological advantage China gains can make it harder for our troops to detect a threat, defend against an attack, protect their communications or accomplish their mission and come home safely. When the CCP develops more capable weapons and more advanced military systems, it is our service members who may ultimately have to face them. Our troops should never have to face a more powerful Chinese military because American dollars helped build it. We are closing loopholes, addressing the ways financial and professional services can help Chinese companies advance, and ensuring that restrictions keep pace with the technologies Beijing is trying to acquire. Because this is not just about money. It is about American lives. That is why we cannot afford to be careless about where American money goes. We cannot warn the American people about China's military buildup with one hand while allowing our capital and expertise to help finance it with the other. Protecting our national security means making difficult decisions, confronting uncomfortable realities and refusing to let short-term financial interests come before the safety of the American people. We also need to recognize that this competition is about more than the next investment or the next regulation. It is about who will control the technologies that shape the future on and off the battlefield. Artificial intelligence (AI), advanced semiconductors, quantum computing and other critical technologies will determine economic strength and military power for generations to come. CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS America has the talent, the resources and the ingenuity to lead that race. But we cannot win if we keep handing our advantages to the Chinese Communist Party. We have the responsibility to protect our breakthroughs, strengthen our defense industrial base and make sure American innovation serves American interests. It’s for this very reason I have been so passionate about passing legislation to do these very things. During this Congress, we in the House Foreign Affairs Committee have been staunch supporters of codifying the president’s AI Action Plan with legislation such as the AI OVERWATCH Act, the MATCH Act and the Remote Access Security Act, to strengthen oversight of advanced AI chip exports, close loopholes in semiconductor equipment controls and prevent China from bypassing our safeguards through remote access to sensitive technology. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION We cannot let the CCP exploit gaps in our laws to get the chips, equipment and computing power it needs to strengthen its military. If we close one door but leave another wide open, China will always find a way through and it will mean dangerous consequences for the U.S. on the other side. articles.title: GIANNO CALDWELL: I fled California. Steve Hilton gives voters golden opportunity to stay
articles.summary: Steve Hilton's California governor race targets Los Angeles-style decline with bold plans on gas prices, housing and crime across the Golden State.
articles.body: I lived in Los Angeles from 2017 until May 2020, two months into the LA shutdown, and by the end I barely recognized it. The city I had moved to for its energy and opportunity was starting to look like Gotham City. Tent cities spread across Los Angeles. Break-ins and violent crime climbed. When COVID-19 arrived, the people running California seemed far more interested in policing masks on the beach than policing the streets. So, I left for Miami because Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis governed his state with sanity. I was blessed. I could leave. Millions of Californians can't, and they shouldn't have to. Six years later, California Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton is giving Californians a reason to stay. articles.title: Shania Twain headlines State Fayre festival in Chelmsford
articles.summary: The Grammy award-winning star is to perform at an Americana festival which made its debut this year.
articles.body:
Country pop music icon Shania Twain has been revealed as the first headliner for next year's second edition of an Americana music festival in Essex.

The five-time Grammy-award winner will perform at State Fayre in Hylands Park, Chelmsford, on Saturday, 19 June.

The singer, whose hits include Man, I Feel Like A Woman and That Don't Impress Me Much, said she had heard the event, which was held for the first time this summer, was "a blast", adding: "I can't wait to experience it for myself."

Organisers described Twain as "an icon not just in the history of country music, but also in global culture itself" and said she would be "the perfect fit for what State Fayre is all about".

The inaugural event saw performers including Kings of Leon and Alanis Morissette perform at the site, which was formerly home to V Festival and hosted BBC Radio 2 in the Park in September 2025.

State Fayre promoters said more than 50,000 fans attended June's event, which celebrates "Americana culture spanning genres".

Twain, who performed at Glastonbury in the "legends slot" in 2024, said she would be performing her classic hits as well as material from her recently-released album.

"We all know I love the UK and my UK fans are the best," she added.

The Canadian star released her self-titled debut album in 1993 and her 1997 album Come On Over is listed by Guinness World Records as the biggest-selling studio album by a female solo artist with an estimated 40 million copies sold.

articles.title: Sudan files complaints against Ethiopia with UN over deadly drone spree
articles.summary: One-way drone attacks have killed or wounded 484 civilians since February, Khartoum says.
articles.body:
Sudan has lodged a complaint against Ethiopia with both the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council after a series of deadly drone attacks this year.

In a statement late on Sunday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group of using Ethiopian territory to launch “brazen aggression” against “civilian sites and power stations” in Sudan, resulting in hundreds of casualties and disruptions to essential services.

The string of incidents “places Ethiopia before international law”, the ministry added.

Sudan’s military has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of aiding the RSF, which it has been fighting in a civil war since April 2023. Ethiopia, meanwhile, has accused the Sudanese military of backing rebels linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front , a charge Khartoum denied.

The ministry’s statement came alongside a report from Sudan’s army-led Transitional Sovereignty Council that alleged 70 assaults from February 15 to October 27 involving 187 one-way attack drones.

The attacks killed or wounded 484 civilians and killed 176 Sudanese soldiers, the report said, with another 200 soldiers wounded.

“Since February 2026, armed drones have taken off from Ethiopian soil … to strike Sudanese cities and civilians,” the report said.

The report identified launch sites at Asosa Airport in western Ethiopia, the Kurmuk-Gizen border area and Bahir Dar airbase in northwestern Ethiopia’s Amhara region.

Last month saw 28 attacks carried out by 97 drones, the report said.

It cited an October 9 attack on displaced families in Wad el-Mahi, located in Sudan’s Blue Nile region near the Ethiopian border, which it said killed 30 civilians – 26 women and four children – and wounded 100.

A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Saturday that he was “appalled” by the impact of drone strikes in Sudan, days after another strike on a market in RSF-controlled territory in Darfur killed more than 100 people .

The secretary-general “strongly condemns the escalating drone attacks in Sudan by the parties to the conflict and the catastrophic toll these attacks are inflicting on civilians”, the spokesman said, adding that the strikes constitute violations of international humanitarian law.

articles.title: Donovan Marx farm attack: Five arrested after South African farmer shot and tortured
articles.summary: The attack on Donovan Marx, 50, comes as right-wing groups say there is a genocide of white people - a claim widely discredited.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains graphic details that some people may find distressing

South African police have arrested five people in connection with a brutal attack on a cattle farmer, who was assaulted and tortured in what has been described as a "senseless and barbaric" act.

Donovan Marx, 50, was attacked during a house robbery on his farm in Ventersdorp, a small town in South Africa's North West province, last Wednesday.

Marx was ambushed as he returned home, shot and stabbed and had his ears cut off in the horrific ordeal, police said.

All five of his alleged attackers were arrested over the weekend, a move welcomed by Marx's wife and family.

They added that the "legal process must [now] take its course".

The horrific attack has caused widespread outrage in a country which is used to high levels of violence.

Police last week explained how the attack on Mark happened.

A group of masked men armed with guns approached a worker at Mark's house as he was mowing the lawn, they said in a statement.

The attackers then demanded to know where Marx was before tying the worker's hands and feet with cable ties.

When Marx returned home, police said two of the suspects allegedly approached him and shot him in the upper body.

"They [then] dragged him inside the house, tied his hands and feet with cable ties, and allegedly stabbed him."

The suspects then ransacked the house and took three firearms from a safe before escaping with Marx's van.

The ordeal ended after the farm worker managed to free himself and call for assistance.

Marx was rushed to hospital, where he remains, but may need prosthetic ears after surgeons were unable to save his own, local news site IOL reported.

South Africa's Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp condemned the attack on Marx, adding there was no "place in our country for such senseless and barbaric acts".

The chair of parliament's police committee, Ian Cameron, praised police for the swift arrests and called for a "strong, properly investigated case" to follow.

The five suspects, aged between 26 and 56, will appear in local courts on Tuesday and face house robbery, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition charges.

Some right-wing groups have used such attacks on white farmers, who are often from the Afrikaner community, to say there is a genocide against white people in the country - a claim that has been widely discredited.

Although the claims have been dismissed by every political party in the country, including those representing Afrikaners, US President Donald Trump has repeated them and has offered white Afrikaners asylum in the US.

South Africa's latest crime statistics, covering the period between April and June 2026, do not specify how many attacks took place on farms and only recorded one robbery in a rural area.

However, police data show most victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black.

articles.title: Fake warnings of nuclear attack posted on hacked Russian and Ukrainian emergency apps
articles.summary: Emergency warning apps in Russia and Ukraine were hacked overnight Sunday into Monday, according to authorities in both countries. It’s not clear whether the hacking of the apps is linked.
articles.body: Emergency warning apps in Russia and Ukraine were hacked overnight Sunday into Monday, according to authorities in both countries. It’s not clear whether the hacking of the apps is linked. The apps warn the public of missile, drone and other threats. But rather than spread panic, the fake messages appear to have had little impact on war-weary civilians – and instead began to generate some imaginative memes. The messages posted on Ukraine’s public air raid app late on Sunday claimed that the capital Kyiv and other areas were subject to nuclear ⁠and chemical alerts as well as the threat of street combat. Another fake message said Russia’s ⁠hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed. “The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the Ukrainian air force said ‌on Telegram. “There ⁠is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!” The app had been recently updated to show the movement of drones in real time. Stepan Tanasiychuk, who leads Ukraine’s Air Raid Alert project, said Monday it was gradually being restored, with new yellow and red alert levels currently available on the map. “The team is taking additional measures to secure the app in order to prevent similar situations in the future, Tanasiychuk said on Instagram. “We realise how much unnecessary worry and inconvenience this has caused.” In a separate event, ⁠the mobile app of Russia’s emergencies ministry – Emercom – was hit by a “massive cyberattack” early Monday that resulted in ⁠”the spread of false information to the public,” state news agency TASS quoted ⁠the ‌ministry as saying. A fake alert was sent to 33 Russian regions, the ministry said. The message claimed that “NUCLEAR WARHEADS ON P1-SUN DELIVERY SYSTEMS have been launched across ALL regions of Russia,” and added an expletive-laden warning. “The app is currently operational, and its full functionality will be restored by the end of the day,” the emergencies ministry said later Monday. “EMERCOM specialists have analyzed the incident and identified the vulnerability exploited by the attacker.” The ministry played down the significance of the incident, saying that alerts are distributed through regional and municipal systems such as sirens and loudspeakers, SMS messages and media broadcasts. “All electronic resources belonging to our government agencies are under constant threat of cyberattacks,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday. “As technologies, including AI, continue to evolve, the threat of cyberattacks is growing,” he said. Few people appear to have fallen for the false messages. Some suggested it had undermined their trust in official warnings. One Russian user said they had deleted the Emercom app “and I won’t be installing anything like that again. How can they leave apps like this vulnerable? It’s complete nonsense, of course, but what if it weren’t?” Among comments on Instagram among Russian users of the app, one said the fake alert “was written in such a way that it’s impossible to believe it’s real.” Another wrote: “It was hard to believe such nonsense. … How did (the Emergencies ministry) even let this happen.. let themselves get hacked.” “You wake up, open Threads and see tons of posts like this,” another commented. “BUT THANKFULLY IT’S FAKE!” Others joked that they had not even received the warning, with one writing: “This information was reserved for the chosen ones, don’t worry, you’re not important enough to be hacked.” One resident of Kyiv responded to the alert about street fighting by posting: “Good thing our mayor is a boxer.” Another social media post made up a long list of additional threats, including: “Cat invasion – Cats are taking over the city. Hide the sausages. Pancake emergency – The city has run out of pancakes. Stay home. Clown attack – Clowns have been spotted in the city. Do not go outside without a mask. Alien invasion – UFOs are approaching Earth. Prepare for contact.”

articles.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
articles.summary: The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C.
articles.body:
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.

Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.

Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.

Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".

He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.

Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.

"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.

The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).

It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.

In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.

Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.

In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce.

The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.

Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.

A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.

Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".

In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.

A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".

"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.

One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."

The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.

Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.

In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.

The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.

The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.

In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.

A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.

A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

articles.title: Discarded racing tyres have become a 17-foot-tall sculpture at an Ohio park, where artist Chakaia Booker unveiled her new work in October 2026, turning racing waste into a public landmark
articles.summary: Discarded racing tyres that once belonged to Goodyear have found a second life as a towering public artwork in Akron, Ohio, a city known for its long
articles.body: Discarded racing tyres that once belonged to Goodyear have found a second life as a towering public artwork in Akron, Ohio, a city known for its long association with the rubber industry. Internationally acclaimed sculptor Chakaia Booker unveiled her 17-foot-tall sculpture, titled 'Transit', at Lock 3 park on October 29, 2026, turning recycled automotive material into a landmark in the heart of the city, according to local news outlet Signal Akron.Made primarily from donated Goodyear Eagle F1 racing tyres and stainless steel, the sculpture comprises two large, crescent-shaped structures covered with rectangular pieces of rubber arranged in an overlapping, shingle-like pattern. Positioned in a grassy area near South Main Street, the installation overlooks the Ohio & Erie Canal and forms part of Akron’s expanding public art landscape. The work is also the city’s first major contemporary outdoor sculpture by a woman artist, Signal Akron reported. Booker revealed the sculpture’s name during a public dedication ceremony at Lock 3. Addressing the crowd, which gave her a standing ovation, she announced: “The title is ‘Transit’ … and I’m so happy we made it.”The unveiling marked the culmination of a project that began taking shape in 2023, when the Lock 3 Art Task Force selected Booker to create a major work for the park. The concept was subsequently approved by the City of Akron Public Art Commission. Curated Storefront, an organisation that brings contemporary art into public spaces, commissioned the sculpture with support from the city, the Ohio & Erie Canalway Coalition, VIA Art Fund and individual donors, according to Spectrum News 1.Why discarded tyres became the centrepieceBooker’s choice of material has a particular significance in Akron, often called the Rubber Capital of the World. Goodyear was established in the city in the late 19th century, and the tyre industry played a major role in shaping its industrial identity. Using the company’s donated racing tyres for a permanent public artwork connects the city’s manufacturing past with its contemporary cultural ambitions.Heather Meeker, executive director of Curated Storefront, told Spectrum News 1 that Booker’s use of recycled tyres made her an especially appropriate choice for the project. The material, she explained, resonates with generations of Akron residents whose families have worked in the local rubber industry.The sculpture is not simply a collection of tyres stacked together. Its two curved forms and carefully arranged rubber pieces give it a distinctive architectural appearance, while the stainless-steel framework provides structural support. Some pieces of rubber also retain small yellow labels bearing the names of the people who made the tyres, offering visitors a subtle reminder of the workers behind the industrial material.Meeker told Signal Akron that the sculpture contained details that people could continue discovering over time. She expressed hope that generations of Akron residents would enjoy the artwork in the years ahead. The overall project was estimated to cost $550,000, Spectrum News 1 reported.From wearable art to monumental sculpturesFor Booker, 'Transit' represents another chapter in a practice spanning more than four decades. The artist, who was born in New Jersey and lives in New York City, has repeatedly used discarded tyres to create sculptural forms that challenge conventional ideas about waste, texture and artistic materials.Speaking to Signal Akron, Booker traced her introduction to tyres to the 1980s, when she encountered burnt tyres and scraps left behind by car fires. She initially began incorporating the material into wearable art before moving towards sculpture. During the 1990s, she said, her sculptural works grew into larger and more ambitious projects.That evolution is reflected in 'Transit', where material associated with vehicles and industrial production becomes a fixed feature of a public park. Rather than being discarded after its original use, the rubber has been incorporated into an artwork intended to remain accessible to visitors.Booker’s work is held in collections at major institutions, including the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, and New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. Her relationship with Northeast Ohio also predates the Akron commission by more than two decades. She held a solo exhibition at the Akron Art Museum in 2000 and exhibited at the Cleveland Institute of Art in 2015, according to Signal Akron.Dara Harper, a former member of the Lock 3 Art Task Force, said Booker’s established use of tyres was an important factor in the selection process. Harper also highlighted the significance of commissioning a large public work by a woman artist of colour.A new landmark for downtown AkronThe sculpture arrives as Lock 3 continues to develop as a public gathering place. The park reopened in December 2024 after extensive renovations, a $17 million project that included a new performance pavilion, expanded green space and an accessible, winding path, Signal Akron reported. City officials hope Transit will give residents and visitors another reason to explore downtown. Akron Mayor Shammas Malik said the 17-foot installation would add to the experience of visiting a public space intended for everyone.The sculpture’s placement near the canal also links it to the city’s broader efforts to make public art part of its downtown identity. Its scale makes it visible as a landmark, while its recycled materials provide a direct connection to Akron’s industrial heritage.Although the sculpture is made largely from racing tyres, its significance extends beyond the material itself. It brings together manufacturing history, the labour behind an industrial product and a contemporary artist’s long-running interest in transforming discarded objects into large-scale art.You use AI every day. articles.title: French school protests resume on small scale as students return from break
articles.summary: Education ministry says 41 schools blockaded as students return after holiday break.
articles.body:
High school students in France have resumed protests on a much smaller scale than in previous weeks as pupils returned from their two-week holiday break.

The Ministry of Education said 41 high schools were blockaded on Monday, about one percent of the country’s 3,700, according to the French public broadcaster Franceinfo.

Students attempted to blockade schools in Paris, Marseille and Rennes, the Reuters news agency reported. Hundreds of schools were blockaded in the weeks before the break.

“In terms of blockades, or attempted blockades, the phenomenon is very marginal. We’re talking about a handful of units, a few individual schools,” Education Minister Edouard Geffray told France Inter radio. He said protests were allowed, but preventing access to schools was illegal.

“The school year is now at risk for several hundred thousand pupils and we can’t allow that,” Geffray said, according to the state public news service Franceinfo.

The protests began in the Paris suburbs in September and spread across France. Last month, the focus of the anger broadened beyond education to the cost of living, drawing in trade unionists and activists. In a test for President Emmanuel Macron’s minority government, some protests turned into violent clashes with police and riots in several cities, with shops looted.

Students are demanding the renovation of ageing schools, more teachers, more university places and an end to a university admissions system they see as socially unfair.

Last week, the government announced a gradual replacement of the Parcoursup admissions platform by 2028, cancelled planned education job cuts, promised 500 additional posts and a cap of 28 pupils per class in the first year of high school, Franceinfo reported. It also pledged 4 billion euros ($4.47bn) to renovate schools and 15,000 new places in higher education.

Student representatives said the offers were not enough and vowed to continue protesting.

“Of course we’re calling for a blockade,” Pierre Sourzat, president of the student organisation Les Lyceens!, said on Sunday, according to France 24.

The Union Syndicale Lyceenne and Student Union have called for further blockades on Tuesday and Thursday, while the UNEF student union said Tuesday should be a “black day” for universities, with blockades across the country.

articles.title: Iran has a 2-day plan to reopen strait, resume nuclear talks with US, and other Mideast news
articles.summary: Iran said Monday it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the United States, shortening a process originally expect...
articles.body:
Iran said Monday it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the United States, shortening a process originally expected to take seven days.

The U.N. migration agency said more than 300,000 people in Yemen had fled renewed fighting. Israel's military said it was wrapping up a sweeping operation that began after a shooting in Hebron killed two soldiers.

China, meanwhile, is sending a special envoy to Iran, Saudi Arabia and Oman.

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here .

Iran's 2-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, resume nuclear talks

Iran said it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the U.S. if Washington meets its demands.

The announcement came as the region braces for possible renewed fighting, even as Iran's top diplomat said Sunday that he hoped the U.S. would choose "diplomacy over other paths."

Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the U.S. met seven conditions, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Iran now says ships passing through the reopened strait would have to follow a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman and travel under Iranian supervision. Separately, Iranian officials have said the U.S. must lift sanctions on Iranian oil sales and agree to a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said the plan remained the basis for negotiations with Washington through mediators, despite the shorter implementation timeline. "This once again demonstrates Iran's good-faith approach," he added.

Baghaei gave no indication that Tehran had changed its demands or that Washington had accepted its proposal.

More than 300,000 Yemenis have fled fighting, UN says

The U.N. migration agency said the people are struggling to find shelter and life essentials, as aid groups face limited access to those in need.

They have fled as renewed fighting between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed government forces broke a four-year truce, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation in one of the Middle East's poorest countries.

Taiz province, in southwestern Yemen, continues to take in displaced families, but many are fleeing south to Aden, which has now received more than 56,000 people, according to the latest figures by the International Organization for Migration.

"After years of conflict, families in Yemen are being forced to flee yet again, often with little more than the clothes on their backs," Abdusattor Esoev, head of the IOM's mission in Yemen, said Sunday.

"They urgently need shelter, food, clean water and health care. Without more funding, thousands of families could be left without the help they urgently need," he added.

China to send special envoy to Iran and the Gulf

China said Monday it plans to send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters the envoy would focus on easing tensions and promoting regional stability.

The Gulf region "should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict," Chinese President Xi Jinping told Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said on Monday, according to a readout of their meeting.

The move comes as China seeks to expand its influence in the rapidly changing region, which it depends on for a large share of its oil .

Some Israeli forces withdraw from Hebron after massive response to deadly shooting

The Israeli military said Monday that it had concluded an operation in Hebron in the occupied West Bank that began last month after two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers. It said it demolished the gunmen's residences and confiscated weapons and illegal vehicles.

The operation, focused on the area where the shooting took place, displaced hundreds of Palestinians. They began to return home on Monday as some Israeli forces withdrew from one of the most tense cities in the territory .

In Deir Bahha, the suspected gunmen's neighborhood, explosives experts checked for any unexploded devices left behind by soldiers and bulldozers cleared blocked roads. Some residents found their homes were damaged in military raids. "I came back expecting everything to be normal, but I was shocked to find the door broken and the glass shattered," said one resident, Wael Shawar.

"I hadn't done anything. The whole house has been left in chaos," he added.

Another returning resident said she feared bringing her children home. "We are afraid," said Tamara Obei. "We don't know what's happening or whether there are explosives or anything else in the house. The children are already psychologically exhausted."

Two Israeli airstrikes killed two men in southern Gaza early Monday, according to Nasser Hospital, where their bodies were taken. One strike killed a man in his home; the other killed a man in a tent.

The Israeli military did not respond to a request for comment.

Major fighting between Israel and Hamas largely halted under the October 2025 ceasefire. Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes on Gaza that it says target militants, though the strikes regularly kill or injure women and children. Israel says Hamas uses civilians as human shields.

About 1,580 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began, bringing the overall death toll to more than 74,500, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, does not distinguish between civilians and militants.

articles.title: Supermarkets across Europe hit by new fridge cyberattacks
articles.summary: Supermarkets across Europe were hit Monday by a new wave of apparent cyberattacks affecting fridges and freezers.
articles.body: Supermarkets across Europe were hit Monday by a new wave of apparent cyberattacks affecting fridges and freezers. The incidents caused temperature spikes and spoiled food at stores in Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Estonia. It follows a cyberattack in France last month, in which police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit and causing fires and food losses. Authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There were no claims of responsibility. The issues come as the continent confronts broader security fears stemming from Russia’s war in Ukraine. The new cyberattack highlights how digital threats can increasingly affect citizens’ everyday lives, the European Commission said Monday. The Ahold Delhaize supermarket chain in the Netherlands told NBC News on Monday that it was aware of an “IT incident” affecting the refrigeration systems in a number of its stores. “Our teams are working hard to fully assess the situation,” the company said in an email. Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s systems, told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyberattack, in which the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode. A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops had their fridge systems attacked. The Carrefour supermarket chain in the country said a “cyberattack targeting refrigeration installations only had an extremely limited impact,” affecting 15 of its more than 700 stores. Sweden’s grocery retailer chain ICA told NBC News its systems were not affected, but that it had been informed of “an incident at a small number of stores that use an external supplier and have their connectivity outside ICA’s central network.” The incident has affected the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems, the company said in an email. “ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the incident,” it said. The ICA Kvantum branch in Sjöbo in southern Sweden wrote on its Facebook page that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. It said it was working to discard the affected items. Privately held grocery retail group Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents. In Ireland, food wholesaler Musgrave said that a cyber incident had affected refrigeration systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores, forcing it to remove some chilled and frozen products from sale. “Our monitoring systems alerted us to the issue and we took immediate action,” it said in a statement. “Our investigation is ongoing.” The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NBC News. In Estonia, a company that makes the affected technology said that one of its clients had been hit by a cyberattack in which attackers accessed a computer controlling refrigeration and also turned up the temperature to 122 degrees Fahrenheit, public broadcaster ERR reported. From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals. Sweden’s national cybersecurity center — which said it could not speculate on who was behind the attacks — is working on several incidents affecting grocery stores across the country, the head of the center, John Billow, said on Monday. “We have in recent weeks... identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” the cybersecurity center’s Billow said.

articles.title: Al-Jawf becomes new hotspot in Yemen war between government forces, Houthis
articles.summary: Recent military advances by Yemeni government forces highlight the geographic and strategic significance of Al-Jawf.
articles.body:
Al-Jawf has become a new focal point in the conflict between forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis, highlighting the strategic importance of the northern governorate.

A major counteroffensive has been launched by the Yemeni government army and forces loyal to it to capture the strategic heights east of the provincial capital, al-Hazm, from the Houthis.

The operations are part of Operation Dawn of Yemen, launched by the government last month to reverse Houthi territorial gains and restore state control in the country.

Al-Hazm has become a central part of this operation, with the city a potential launchpad for government forces against the Houthis. They have controlled the capital Sanaa and most of northern Yemen since the war broke out in September 2014.

During the 12 years of war in Yemen, control over al-Hazm has shifted several times, with the Houthis seizing the city in March 2020.

The governorate remains highly coveted due to its expansive border with Saudi Arabia and its direct geographic links to five pivotal governorates: Hadramout, Saada, Sanaa, Amran and oil-rich Marib and close to the capital, Sanaa.

Al-Jawf also acts as a vital defensive shield for Marib, controlled by government forces, preventing the Houthis from advancing into the eastern regions. It is also a gateway to major Houthi strongholds in northern Yemen.

Field Commander Colonel Rabie Al-Qurashi said government forces have been able to win complete control over the strategic Huwaishan mountain range, east of al-Hazm city. He said it is the first line of defence for the Houthis in the eastern axis and control over the rugged region would give government forces the ability to disrupt rebel supply routes.

“Government forces succeeded in breaking that defensive format with partial control over the Al-Alam front road,” Al-Qurashi said. “The government advance represents a beginning to tighten the noose on the Houthis in the upper al-Labanat camp,” which is regarded as a vital eastern gateway to Sanaa.

Ali Al-Dahab, a military and strategic affairs researcher, said there are immense tactical benefits from holding this elevated terrain.

“The recent advances of government forces in Al-Jawf are a military transformation that serves the course of future operations for their arrival to al-Hazm city,” Al-Dahab told Al Jazeera.

“The government forces’ recovery of a number of heights there provides a military and psychological morale advantage and confuses the Houthis’ decisions, in addition to granting government forces monitoring, movement, and observation of Houthi supply lines and securing their own lines.”

Military spokesman Majed Abdullah Al-Nuzaili said on X that recent military operations against Houthi positions in al-Jawf were “inflicting losses on the militia’s capabilities”.

The government dominates the vast eastern desert district of Khabb wa ash Sha’af, representing 82 percent of the governorate’s total area. The Houthis control the provincial capital, al-Hazm, and 10 other districts.

Security and political affairs researcher Brigadier General Ahmed Al-Awadhi stressed the importance of “continuous but not rapid” government advances in the area.

“The advances of government forces in Al-Jawf cannot be ignored or their importance underestimated,” Al-Awadhi told Al Jazeera.

“Control over heights or mountain ranges in the desert Al-Jawf governorate represents points of military strength regardless of their proximity to or distance from the governorate capital.”

The government forces advances in al-Jawf highlight a historical vulnerability for the Houthis, having suffered repeated defeats in battles in desert and open areas, he added.

The developments coincide with the Presidential Council’s appointment of Major General Amin Ali Al-Akimi as governor and military commander of al-Jawf.

“[His] reappointment… comes within the context of restructuring the theatre of operations and unifying the front,” Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen-focused analyst told Al Jazeera.

“Hailing from Dhu Hussein, a branch of the Daham Bakil tribe, Al-Akimi possesses tribal and military influence that could help mobilise tribes, overcome divisions and bolster momentum on the ground. However, translating this influence into sustainable gains remains contingent upon unifying command and control, coordinating operations across all battlefronts, securing military and logistical support and strengthening anti-corruption efforts to improve the efficient management of military resources.”

The Houthis say they have thwarted advances by government forces in al-Jawf and Marib.

Fighting has continued in other parts of Yemen as Houthi-affiliated media reported air strikes on an oil company facility in the Bajil district of Hodeidah, which coincide with fierce fighting further south.

Government forces repelled Houthi attacks in al-Aqroudh and on the Tur al-Baha front in Lahij governorate. Intense fighting continues in Taiz governorate.

The siege of Taiz City continues to strain medical infrastructure, with deliveries of food and fuel severely restricted. Civilians remain at risk from sniper fire from surrounding hillsides, authorities have warned.

Governor Nabil Shamsan said that hospitals are working at only 20 percent capacity, with 120 health centres entirely shut due to the siege.

“We urge the international community to secure at least one safe route between Taiz and Aden to enable citizen movement and the smooth entry of services, essential materials and goods,” Shamsan appealed to Al Jazeera.

More than 300,000 people have fled their homes in western Yemen due to the escalating fighting, leaving civilians highly vulnerable.

articles.title: Jordan’s King Abdullah promises to confront ‘terrorists’ after Karak attack
articles.summary: King tells parliament attackers ‘are not of us’ and warns that Israeli expansionism is greatest threat to the region.
articles.body:
Jordan’s King Abdullah II says the kingdom would not be shaken by a deadly attack on a church in the southern city of Karak last month.

Opening a new session of parliament in the capital, Amman, on Monday, Abdullah said “the treacherous hand of terrorism” had reached out “to test the resilience of our state and the resolve of our people”.

“They are not of us,” he said of the attackers. “There is no place for them among us, not today and not tomorrow.”

The attack about two weeks ago killed nine people and wounded dozens. The king asked lawmakers to stand for a minute of silence for the victims, whose relatives attended the session.

Al Jazeera’s Ahmed Jarrar, reporting from Amman, said Abdullah made clear that Jordan would confront “terrorism and extremism” by relying first on national unity and public awareness, backed by the army and security services, which would strike “with an iron fist”.

Abdullah also addressed regional tensions, warning that Israeli expansionism is the greatest threat to the Middle East.

“Israeli expansionist ambitions are the greatest threat to the future of the region and its security,” he said, adding: “The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza continues, and successive assaults persist in the West Bank and Jerusalem.”

The king also pledged to protect Jordan’s scarce water supplies, Jarrar said.

“We will not allow the thirst of Jordanians to be held hostage by any party,” he said. Jarrar said this reflected concerns that Israeli projects threaten the kingdom’s water security.

Jordan, a close United States ally, signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994, and millions of its citizens are of Palestinian origin.

Jarrar said the king’s third message was directed at lawmakers as he stressed that the nation is the source of authority and debate in parliament is healthy as long as it serves the national interest.

“Your differences of opinion are a strength so long as Jordan’s interest is the goal,” Abdullah said, urging the government to improve living conditions.

He also warned officials against abusing their positions. “The law knows no name, no position and no influence,” he said.

articles.title: Public's help needed to solve mystery of starling murmurations
articles.summary: People are invited to take part in research into why starlings form murmurations before they roost.
articles.body:
Starling murmurations are described as some of the "most amazing spectacles" to witness and they happen just before the birds go down to roost - but the reason why they do it is still uncertain.

A decade on from a study into the behaviour, researchers at University of Gloucestershire are repeating the research and inviting the public to take part in a new, nationwide study.

Lead researcher Prof Anne Goodenough said they were interested in seeing what had "changed in the past decade, particularly because starlings are a declining species".

Information on where and when displays occur, the size and duration and whether birds of prey are present, is what researchers are looking to gather.

How can heritage buildings be brought back into use?

Museum wing reopens after four-year project

City status will not be lost in shake-up - minister

The original study found there was an average of 30,000 birds in a murmuration, while some of the larger ones had more than 750,000 birds, with sightings from 23 countries.

One of the central mysteries surrounding murmurations is why starlings gather in such enormous, tightly coordinated flocks before going to roost.

The research from 10 years ago backed the idea that murmurations are primarily to protect them against predators such as peregrine falcons and sparrowhawks.

"The only way that we can complete this research is by everybody submitting records as and when they see them," said Goodenough.

Due to "habitat change" there had been a "decrease in the population over the last 10 years and we're interested to see what and how that might have affected starling murmuration behaviour", she added.

For the new study, members of the public are invited to report murmurations they see during the autumn and winter through an online survey .

Prof Adam Hart, co-author of the original study, said "the great thing about this project is that almost anyone can contribute".

"Simple observations from thousands of people can tell us more about this remarkable behaviour," they added.

articles.title: Huntingdon train attacker said 'I am the baddest', trial hears
articles.summary: Police responded to fears about Anthony Williams on a train the day before the attack, jurors hear.
articles.body:
A man accused of a mass train stabbing was heard saying "I am the baddest, no-one is as bad as me", on a different train the day before the attack, a court has heard.

Anthony Williams is accused of attempting to murder 10 people on a London-bound train which had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire on 1 November last year.

A passenger texted the British Transport Police reporting a male behaving erratically the night before, Cambridge Crown Court heard.

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder over events on the train, and beforehand in Peterborough and London.

He is accused of trying to kill three people in Peterborough during the evening of 31 October. Later that night he boarded a train from the city's railway station, headed towards London.

In a statement read to jurors, another passenger, Keirah Lee-Oakman, said a male entered the train, sat down and "appeared to be talking and mumbling to himself".

She said he began walking up and down the carriages stating "boom and power", repeatedly saying things like "I haven't got it" as well as referencing the devil, jurors were told.

Lee-Oakman said he was "acting in an aggressive and intimidating manner... I felt unsafe" and while on the train she sent a text to the British Transport Police.

Jurors heard police officers attended Stevenage station but the male dropped down on to the tracks and officers eventually deemed it unsafe to continue following him.

Abbie Harrison-Evans was on the train with her partner Ethan Daniels. She said there was a "male shouting from the front of the train" who was "playing spooky Halloween music on his phone".

His behaviour was "erratic" and her "first impression was he was suffering from a mental condition", the court heard.

She sent a Snapchat to Daniels stating "we going to get attacked or what?".

Harrison-Evans said Williams had a black rucksack on the seat next to him and "kept grabbing it and saying 'I'm going to do it'."

"It looked like he was reaching for something inside the black rucksack," she said.

The court heard Williams said "I'm going to do it, I'm going to do it", followed by "I cannot do it", and she had a "feeling he was going to hurt us".

Daniels said he heard the man state: "I am the baddest, no-one is as bad as me."

Williams is also accused of attempting to murder Isaiah Idris on a Docklands Light Railway train in London in the early hours of 1 November.

In a video recorded interview played to jurors, Idris said: "Only a couple of seconds after the train started moving, he sliced my face.

"When he sliced me… I didn't know at first, I didn't feel anything." He later saw blood "dripping down my face".

He said the man repeatedly asked "are you beefing the devil?", and tried to attack him again, before the victim blocked him with his hand.

Idris said that when the train stopped and the doors opened, the man "turned around and ran away".

Williams is accused of attempting to murder Raza Aslam, Sachin Balakrishnan, Scott Bletcher, Stephen Crean, Kevin Deely, Jonathan Gjoshe, Scott Green, Michael Paffett, David Presland and Samir Zitouni on the London-bound train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on 1 November.

The trial has been told that whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question, but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals.

articles.title: Fridges hacked, food spoiled: Cyberattack disrupts supermarkets across Europe
articles.summary: A suspected cyberattack targeting supermarket refrigeration systems has affected stores in Belgium, Estonia, Sweden and Ireland, forcing retailers to
articles.body: A suspected cyberattack targeting supermarket refrigeration systems has affected stores in Belgium, Estonia, Sweden and Ireland, forcing retailers to discard large quantities of spoiled food after the temperatures of fridges and freezers were remotely raised.European commissioner for agriculture and food Christophe Hansen on Monday described the attacks as “a deliberate attempt to disrupt” the European Union’s food supply and undermine consumers’ confidence in it. He said food security was not currently at risk, but warned that “the food waste and impact on businesses are real”.The incident, reported overnight between Sunday and Monday, has hit several major supermarket chains, including Delhaize and Carrefour in Belgium, ICA and Coop in Sweden, and SuperValu in Ireland. Thirteen SuperValu stores were affected, while around 40 Delhaize outlets and 15 Carrefour stores in Belgium reported problems.In Belgium, some refrigeration units were reportedly set to as high as 70 degrees Celsius, causing an estimated €100,000 worth of food to be discarded at one Delhaize branch alone, according to local media reports. The total losses across affected stores could run into millions of euros, although a consolidated estimate has not been released.Carrefour Belgium spokesman Mich Vergauwen described the incident as a cyberattack, saying there was no other explanation, but added that its impact had been limited. The company said only 15 stores were affected and that it had taken immediate measures to keep its outlets operational.Delhaize also confirmed an IT incident involving refrigeration systems at several dozen stores. “We immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational,” a company spokesperson told Euronews.Fridges remotely reset, food thrown awayThe impact extended to Sweden, where several ICA supermarkets reported that their refrigeration systems had been compromised. One store in Sjöbo, in the country's south, said on social media that its fridges and freezers had been hacked overnight and their temperatures set to 50 degrees Celsius. The outlet temporarily closed before reopening.An ICA spokesperson said the incident had affected a small number of stores operating outside the chain’s central network, adding that the company was helping them manage the situation.Seven of Sweden’s 800 Coop stores were also affected. The retailer told the BBC that the situation was contained and under control.In Ireland, supermarket group Musgrave said 13 SuperValu stores had been hit by a suspected cyberattack. In Luxembourg, Delhaize suspended its ordering systems as a precaution.Belgium’s refrigeration installer Sabcobel said it had identified around 20 affected units among the hundreds it manages in the country. Its chief executive, Stephan Moelans, told Belga that the Belgian attack appeared to use the same mechanism as a cyberattack on French supermarkets in October.In Estonia, a hacker accessed a computer controlling refrigeration at one Selver supermarket and changed a freezer setting to 50 degrees Celsius above zero. The attack was detected within minutes and caused no damage to products, the retailer said.Similar attack hit French supermarkets last monthA cyberattack on October 12 that affected hundreds of supermarkets in France belonging to the Intermarché and Coopérative U chains. That attack also targeted refrigeration systems, causing temperatures to rise and food to spoil.Moelans said refrigeration companies had been working to protect customers against the vulnerability since the French incident, but warned that a software update alone would not be enough. Physical modifications to the systems were also required, he said.“The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection,” Moelans told Euronews, adding that many of Sabcobel’s customers had switched to this arrangement after the attack in France.The identity of those behind the latest attack remains unclear. articles.title: Mamdani says Trump agrees to grant visa to mother of Ghanian teen killed in Bronx shooting
articles.summary: Fifteen-year-old Javits Frimpong was on his way to school in a Bronx neighborhood shortly before 9:30 a.m. Thursday when he was shot in the abdomen, police said.
articles.body: NEW YORK — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Saturday in a social media post that after talking to President Donald Trump, he has agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a 15-year-old immigrant from Ghana who was shot to death earlier this week. The White House did not immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press confirming the administration would be issuing the visa. The teen, Javits Frimpong, was on his way to school in a Bronx neighborhood shortly before 9:30 a.m. Thursday when he was shot in the abdomen, New York City police said. He was pronounced dead at a hospital later that day. No arrests have yet been made, and the killing remains under investigation. “The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away,” Mamdani wrote Saturday on X. “Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately.” “All of New York City is mourning this tragedy,” he said. Frimpong arrived in the Bronx from Ghana a year ago to be with his father and begin a new life in the United States, according to U.S. Rep. Ritchie Torres, a Democrat from the Bronx. Frimpong was on his way to school when he was shot, Torres wrote on X. “Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him,” Torres said. “Every child in the Bronx deserves to walk to school without fearing for their life, and no parent should ever have to endure what Javits’s father, Thomas, is enduring now.” Thomas Frimpong described his son as a quiet teen who spent much of his time on his cellphone. He told reporters that several days before the shooting he learned his son was being bullied at school. “It was the principal who told me,” Thomas Frimpong said. “He said two guys are disturbing my son so he has suspended the two guys. My son is at school. He’s innocent, so I call him. I talk with my son, he said ‘dad, I’m OK.’” Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa said in a post on X that Ghanaian officials in New York are coordinating with local authorities and that the foreign ministry “will work tirelessly with U.S. authorities to ensure justice is secured.” Trump has clamped down on immigration during his second term, including suspending the processing of visas from 75 countries.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy returns to court as defense seeks to block retrial in murder case
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three children in 2023, will be back in court Monday for a hearing that could determine whether she will face a retrial.
articles.body: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three children in 2023, will be back in court Monday for a hearing that could determine whether she will face a retrial. Her defense team argued Monday that she can’t be retried on double jeopardy grounds, meaning a defendant cannot be prosecuted twice for the same crime, in a bid to have the charges dismissed. In court, defense attorney Martin Weinberg argued that the prosecution must prove that the manifest necessity standard was met to warrant a mistrial and, in turn, a retrial. But Weinberg said the defense team believes there first should have been a voir dire, or questioning, of the holdout juror “which could have established further that the reasons were personal, rather than simply because of the internal chemistry of jury deliberations.” That questioning, Weinberg argued, could have led to the juror being discharged, allowing deliberations to continue with another juror, “and that’s the viable alternative that we claim countered the manifest necessity that the rule requires for double jeopardy,” he said in court. In response, Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said the court must determine whether manifest necessity was met based on what happened in court and what the court knew at the time, not on information revealed in the media after the trial. “Your decision to declare it in this trial should be assessed based on what happened here in this courtroom,” Sprague told the judge. “In cases where a mistrial had already been declared, it is clear from the record that this juror did not refuse to deliberate; he refused to agree.” In a motion Thursday, the prosecution asked the judge to reject Clancy’s motion to dismiss charges against her, arguing they have a right to seek justice for her three slain children, even though the first trial ended in a mistrial in September. The defense team is also expected to try to argue for reduced charges as an alternative, which could pave the way for a bench trial instead of a second jury trial. Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, however, indicated in the last week of the trial that he was ready to start a retrial as soon as possible. Days after the judge declared a mistrial in the state case, he also asked President Donald Trump to pardon his client. Presidents can pardon only federal offenses. The defense will also argue to preserve juror records and to investigate the lone holdout juror, whom other jurors have said was the sole roadblock to a unanimous decision. Prosecutors are expected to file a motion Monday that bars lawyers and law enforcement involved in the case from speaking to the media. Clancy is accused of strangling her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months old — with exercise bands on the evening of Jan. 24, 2023, before throwing herself out of her bedroom window in a suicide attempt that left her paralyzed and in a wheelchair. During her trial, Reddington argued that Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis and was compelled to act on auditory hallucinations when she carried out the killings. Prosecutors, however, have said she was aware of her actions and planned the murders ahead of time. She was not actually in psychosis when she killed the children, they said. It remains unclear whether both sides will argue the same fact patterns if there is a retrial. The jury deadlocked three times, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial, despite Reddington’s best efforts to attempt a last-minute emergency stay. Supreme Judicial Court Associate Justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt later denied it. The foreperson reported one holdout, who they said was not following the law of “beyond a reasonable doubt.” Jurors have since spoken out, with several pointing to one juror they said would not uphold the reasonable-doubt standard and was the only one of 12 jurors who wanted to convict Clancy. They said he would not engage in discussions and failed to provide evidence to support his reasoning. The lone juror, Michael P. Desronvil, has since said he has felt harassed since the end of the trial and insisted he “didn’t have any doubts.” The trial captivated the nation as online sleuths peddled conspiracy theories that Clancy was not the one who killed the children. Rather, that her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, carried out the murders and framed her for it. In a statement following the first trial, Patrick Clancy’s lawyers slammed true-crime creators pushing the theories and called them a “campaign of misinformation” that was “publishing what they know to be outright falsehoods that Patrick was somehow involved in the death of his young children and other vile claims.” The lawyers added that “every appropriate measure will be pursued to hold them accountable, including legally” and that “law enforcement has been notified.” Patrick Clancy testified for the prosecution in the first trial, detailing the horrors he found at his home when he returned from running errands the night of the murders. He has also filed a civil suit against Clancy’s doctors, alleging that misdiagnoses and several prescription medications worsened her condition. Reddington told NBC News that Clancy rejects those conspiracy theories about her ex-husband. “She knows, and it’s readily apparent that Patrick has been set upon and his life has been turned upside down into a nightmare that he doesn’t deserve. Period. Full stop,” Reddington said in September. He added that after the trial, Clancy “was not very good” and remained “suicidal.” “She’s strong. She has incredible family support,” he said of his client. “But she is suicidal. I mean, she’s on 24/7, one-on-one suicide watch. I worry about her every day.”

articles.title: How would Tehran respond if the US and Israel bomb Iran again?
articles.summary: Iran has retained significant offensive capability, but civilians and critical infrastructure remain largely exposed.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s military is warning that if all-out war breaks out again with the United States and Israel, it will be longer and more costly than their rivals expect.

Iran’s armed forces could deploy new weapons and tactics against the US, Israel and other countries, which would be the third major conflict between the countries since June last year.

There have been increasing signs that the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which began on February 28, could restart after the US midterm elections. President Donald Trump said on Sunday that the war with Iran will end “very soon one way or the other” and Tehran should agree a deal or “the hammer” will come down.

Hossein Kanani Moghaddam, a former senior IRGC commander, told Al Jazeera that despite extensive blows to the Iranian armed forces during US and Israeli strikes earlier this year, they are now in better operational shape compared with previous conflicts.

“In terms of offence, our target database has significantly expanded, the range, accuracy and warheads of our missiles have improved and our drone capabilities have increased,” he said.

New enemy assets were being identified and operations in additional geographical areas were being planned, he added. Arkaminia said that previously undisclosed capabilities and targets would be revealed – and used – if Iran is attacked again.

Commanders from Iran’s General Staff of Armed Forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Islamic Republic of Iran Army are reported to have recently met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to discuss what steps will be taken if attacked again. The response will be immediate and could go beyond the West Asia region , they said.

The IRGC was “100 percent ready” to confront another attack, spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said on Sunday evening, describing “maximum deterrence” as a goal Iran would reach in the near future.

Army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said the commanders would rely on “asymmetric warfare” tactics that would compensate for the superiority of US military equipment.

He added that “some weaponry was renovated and new equipment was added along with new tactics” during the brief ceasefire period that came after the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US.

Last month, state television showed an underground drone production line. The authorities also showcased an upgraded version of the Arash attack drone and claimed that its warhead had doubled to 100kg with improved guidance.

According to a Reuters investigation published last week, numerous military agencies linked with Iran’s defence establishment have evaded sanctions and funnelled billions into military imports to replenish the IRGC. The imports between January 2025 and June this year from China, Russia and Germany to fuel missile and drone production included rocket propellants, explosives, detonators, titanium and heavy-duty trucks that could be used as launchers.

Many Iranian missile defence systems, radars and other equipment were hit during the war. But Kanani Moghaddam said remaining and newly developed systems were becoming more accurate, pointing to the targeting of a US-built F-35 and other warplanes and drones as successes that can be replicated and expanded upon.

“At sea, we have shown that we can easily target supertankers,” he said regarding transit through the Strait of Hormuz that is deemed “unauthorised” by Iranian authorities. He said Iranian attacks on US Navy vessels in September prompted them to stop venturing into the critical waterway since. But the US has continued its naval blockade on southern Iranian ports, while Iran’s civilian population and infrastructure remain largely exposed if the war resumes.

Tehran and other cities across the country lack shelters or early warning systems to protect civilians. Authorities have not reported any progress regarding the promised shelters and gaps in public warning arrangements.

Iran’s electricity grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, petrochemical and steel manufacturers and roads and railways could also be attacked again, making life even more difficult amid the economic crisis.

During both wars, many senior political and military figures of the Islamic Republic were killed by US and Israeli strikes.

The new supreme leader has not been seen or heard from since replacing his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in early March, ostensibly for security reasons.

This has led to tighter domestic security controls, and prompted some voices from within the establishment to raise concerns and demand accountability for intelligence failures and protection of leadership.

“We have been hit and hit hard,” state-linked analyst Hamzeh Rahim Safavi said during a televised debate on Saturday. “The main cause is intelligence weakness, but no one talks about it or is held accountable”.

The analyst is the son of Yahya Rahim Safavi, a former commander-in-chief of the IRGC who currently serves as a senior military adviser to the supreme leader. The analyst said calls by hardliners to acquire a nuclear bomb would not repair intelligence and security weaknesses.

But Esmaeil Kowsari, a former IRGC division commander now a parliamentary national-security commission member, told local media last week that even though the supreme leader and others were assassinated, “the enemies did not reach their main goals”. He said the goals were to overthrow the Islamic Republic and fragment Iran.

“On the eve of their elections, the Americans are trying to pretend that they have achieved victory by causing a ruckus and launching psychological operations, but that is not the truth,” Kowsari said.
