articles.title: Panchkula, Haryana: Shock and anger in India after eight-year-old beats six-year-old in school
articles.summary: The girl, who was seriously injured, is out of danger, but remains traumatised by her assault, her family said.
articles.body:
Warning: Some details in this story could be distressing for some readers.

There has been shock and anger in India over video footage from the CCTV of a school that shows an eight-year-old boy brutally beating a six-year-old girl.

The girl, who was seriously injured, is recovering in hospital and is now out of danger but remains traumatised by the assault in Haryana state, her family has said.

Police say they have registered a case and the eight-year-old has been sent to a home for juvenile offenders where he is undergoing psychiatric evaluation.

The school principal and two other teachers have been suspended for suspected negligence, police say.

The incident that took place in a government school in Panchkula in the northern state of Haryana on 28 October came to light at the weekend after the CCTV footage went viral on social media.

The horrific assault has sent shock waves through the country. Many people expressed anguish over the little girl's injuries - and the brutality displayed by the boy.

Police say the eight-year-old, who is studying in third grade, told the girl that her father was waiting for her in a classroom where he assaulted her.

The family of the girl, who studies in kindergarten, reached the school after being informed by an auto-rickshaw driver that he had gone to pick her up but could not find her.

"When the girl was not found even after school ended, we went in to look for her. No one there knew where she was," her father told BBC Punjabi.

He said the boy who assaulted his daughter told him that she was in a classroom upstairs, where he found his seriously injured daughter.

"When I saw her, I almost screamed. Looking at her condition, I thought they'd killed my daughter. If a child isn't safe in school, then where will she be safe?"

The girl was initially taken to a local hospital but later moved to the multi-speciality PGIMER hospital in the nearby city of Chandigarh.

A statement from PGIMER said the six-year-old girl was "brought to the hospital with critical injuries".

She is under the care of a multidisciplinary team of specialists, which is closely monitoring her condition and providing all necessary medical attention, the hospital said.

"The circumstances involving this little child are deeply concerning. We want to ensure that she receives the best possible medical care, along with all the support and comfort she needs," the statement quoted hospital director Vivek Lal as saying.

The hospital later shared a photo of Dr Lal with the girl sitting in her father's lap and smiling.

In a video statement on Saturday, senior police official Aditi Singh said they had registered an FIR (first information report) against the school management for "negligence" and were investigating what happened.

"The boy is being evaluated by mental experts under the Juvenile Justice Act and further action will be taken accordingly," she added.

Under Indian law, an eight-year-old cannot be punished or sent to jail so the child has been sent to an observation home run by the Juvenile Justice Board, another senior police official Amarinder Singh said.

The emphasis in cases involving minors is on reformation and counselling, he added.

Meanwhile, the Haryana state government has formed a committee to investigate what happened and whether there was any negligence in the case.

articles.title: Karl Bushby completes 28-year, 31,000-mile walk around world and returns to mother’s house
articles.summary: HULL, England — Karl Bushby completed his 28-year odyssey to walk around the world Monday by returning to his mother’s home in northern England.
articles.body: HULL, England — Karl Bushby completed his 28-year odyssey to walk around the world Monday by returning to his mother’s home in northern England. Bushby embraced his emotional mother, Angela, outside her row house in Hull, England, which he left in 1998. They were surrounded by journalists, a documentary film crew and a large crowd outside the home that had a banner saying “Welcome Home Son.” Bushby was a 29-year-old ex-paratrooper when he walked away from the home to a Royal Air Force base near Oxford and caught a flight to South America. He returned as a 57-year-old — softer, grayer and weathered, but far more worldly. “They say it takes a village but literally it took a world to get me here,” Bushby said. “The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation states to get me back here today. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth.” Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, on Nov. 1, 1998, and has walked 31,000 miles across four continents and 30 countries to get home. He navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel to avoid taking a boat or plane — or any transport — to propel him forward. On the final leg of the journey, helicopter footage showed Bushby ringed by supporters as he pushed his cart toward home after getting a hero’s welcome earlier at City Hall. “Sorry to keep you waiting,” he joked to the crowd in the city center. “Is that it, is it done?” He had a thirst for adventure, but his mission only came into focus when his father, Keith, sent him a birthday card in the mid-90s. His dad, an army veteran himself, mentioned an argument among his fellow special forces troops about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge, believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels. Perilous jungles, scorching deserts and frozen tundra slowed him down, but bureaucratic red tape often brought his adventure to a halt for long periods. Bushby originally calculated the distance could be covered in about five years, but he knew that was unrealistic. “You just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that,” he said. “We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years.” He dodged war in the dangerous Darién Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America in 2001, and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama. After being airlifted to safety during the 56-mile Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, they started again and faced a standoff with a polar bear, survived near-death plunges into freezing waters and almost lost all their supplies when their sleds plunged in the sea. After managing the rare crossing, the pair were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally. It took Bushby almost 10 years to make his way through Russia in fits and starts because of visa struggles and weather that only allowed travel a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork. Bushby planned to meet with family, including his son, Adam, whom he has only seen a few times over the journey. He was expected to meet his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time. Then he was off to push his two-wheeled cart the final steps across Hull and reunite with his mother, Angela, whom he hadn’t seen in a decade. “It’s been a week of lasts,” Bushby told the crowd. “The last day in the tent. The last day on the road. After 28 years you couldn’t ask for more than this. This is the last of the last few steps almost to my mother’s house.”

articles.body: Astonishing photographs of rainbows, lightning strikes and incredible cloud formations are among the finalists in the Weather Photographer of the Year 2026 competition. Now it’s up to the public to choose the winner, with voting open until November 5. “This competition continues to show us just how powerful photography can be in connecting people with weather and our changing climate,” Liz Bentley, chief executive of the RMetS, said in the statement. “The incredible images shortlisted this year don’t just showcase the breathtaking, dramatic beauty of our skies, they also serve as a critical reminder of the impacts of climate change,” she added. articles.title: 'Simplification, Solution, Satisfaction': Uttarakhand CM Dhami outlines governance mantra in Khatima
articles.summary: KHATIMA: Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Monday met with residents and elected representatives at the Lohiahead Helipad in Khatima to
articles.body: KHATIMA: Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Monday met with residents and elected representatives at the Lohiahead Helipad in Khatima to hear their grievances, directing administrative officials to redress all issues on a priority basis.Emphasising administrative accountability and responsiveness, the Chief Minister instructed officials that the time-bound disposal of public complaints must be accorded the highest urgency.Reiterating his government's administrative philosophy, Dhami said the state administration operates on the core principle of "Simplification, Solution, and Satisfaction" (Saralikaran, Samadhan, aur Santushti). He directed district officials to ensure that procedural hurdles do not cause unnecessary delays in delivering citizen-centric services.During the interaction, the Chief Minister also held deliberations with local representatives regarding ongoing development works and infrastructure requirements in the area.He reiterated the state government's commitment to expediting regional development projects and enhancing civic amenities for the welfare of the public.Earlier in the day, Dhami inaugurated a newly upgraded Model Primary School in his ancestral village of Nagla Tarai during a one-day visit to his hometown of Khatima, dedicating the modernised educational facility to the local community.Addressing the gathering after the inauguration, the Chief Minister took a walk down memory lane, fondly recalling that he had received his own primary education at the very same school. Emphasising that education plays a foundational role in shaping the future of the youth, Dhami termed the settlement, located along the Indo-Nepal border, the "first village of India."Reflecting on his childhood memories, he said, "This school holds a deeply personal connection for me as I received my primary education here. Today, dedicating this revamped model structure to the community brings immense satisfaction. Education is the key to empowering our children, and our government is consistently working to transform educational infrastructure so that students in every corner of Uttarakhand, particularly in border villages, have access to modern learning environments."During his address, the Chief Minister highlighted several initiatives undertaken by the state government to upgrade school infrastructure and improve learning outcomes across Uttarakhand.Dhami reiterated the state's resolve to ensure that children from rural and border regions are equipped with state-of-the-art facilities to compete on an equal footing.(With ANI inputs)Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news. articles.title: DR ANNIE ANDREWS: South Carolina should expect more from their senator
articles.summary: Dr. Annie Andrews details her Taxpayer Pledge, vowing to ban stock trading, end congressional pensions and make no tax on tips permanent.
articles.body: Throughout this race, I’ve said it plainly: whether you voted for Donald Trump, Lindsey Graham, or anyone else, if you care more about your bills than Washington’s political games, this campaign is for you. I mean it. Last week in Aiken, I stood in a room full of Republicans and independents. One man told me he’d been a Reagan Republican his whole life and had never voted for a Democrat. He came anyway. He wanted to know if I’d actually listen. I’ve been listening for 18 months on the campaign trail, and for 20 years before that in my exam room. INDEPENDENT VOTERS AREN’T PICKING A POLITICAL TEAM, THEY JUST FEEL PICKED ON I didn’t set out to become a politician. I’m a pediatrician and a mom of three. I’ve cared for children whose parents had to choose between groceries and an inhaler, and I’ve taken the 2 a.m. calls from scared moms and dads. Medicine taught me that you show up, you listen, and you make hard decisions under pressure. I’ve traveled to all 46 counties. In Barnwell, I sat on the back of a pickup truck with eighth-generation farmers hurt by tariffs. In Ridgeland, I stood with veterans who have lost friends to suicide and want this war in Iran to end. In Marlboro County, I met a little boy growing up without a hospital because of where he lives. In Myrtle Beach, a 26-year Marine veteran and lifelong Republican came to one of our events after someone encouraged him to attend. Afterward, he told me he’d just made his first political donation. When I ask when they last saw a senator in their hometown, they laugh. They deserve better. This week, Fox News moved our race to a toss-up. Former Republican Gov. David Beasley endorsed me, and more than 100 South Carolina Republican leaders have joined our campaign. They don’t agree with me on everything, but they know I’ll put South Carolina ahead of any party or special interest. My opponent, Darline Graham, has my deepest sympathy for the loss of her brother. articles.title: Displaced in Hebron: Picking up pieces after Israeli siege
articles.summary: Displaced Hebron families return to damaged homes, left to pick up scattered pieces of their lives after Israeli siege.
articles.body:
Hebron, occupied West Bank – Nour al-Natsha knew there was a chance his home wouldn’t be in the best condition upon his return after 10 days of displacement.

Israeli forces had taken over Hebron’s al-Jalada neighbourhood on October 24, a day after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers nearby. Al-Natsha’s family were given 20 minutes to leave, taking only their money, gold and important documents, and leaving behind most of their clothes, everyday belongings and family photographs.

After hearing that Israeli forces had withdrawn , al-Natsha tentatively returned to check on the house on Monday.

He found the doors wide open, and the house turned upside down. Belongings were missing, as well as his young daughter’s pet bird.

“When we entered the house, it was a mixture of emotions,” the 35-year-old orthopaedic surgeon said. “You couldn’t tell whether you were happy to be back home or heartbroken by what had happened to it.”

The Israeli military operation in Hebron appears to be over – but al-Natsha and his family, and thousands of others in the city, are left to pick up the pieces.

Al-Natsha explained that families and neighbours had gathered on Sunday evening in the nearby Wadi al-Karm area, close to their homes, waiting until around midnight after reports emerged that the military operation had ended. But seeing no signs of a withdrawal, they returned to their temporary accommodation, despite holding on to the hope of going home soon.

Then, in the early hours of the morning, it was confirmed that the military had withdrawn. Al-Natsha decided to head towards the neighbourhood at around 6am. There, he found several neighbours making their way home and waited for relatives to arrive before entering the area and inspecting their houses.

Al-Natsha was initially accompanied by his father and two brothers as they inspected the property, looking for suspicious objects or potential hazards after finding the doors open.

Once they were satisfied that the house was safe, family members began cleaning and putting things back in order, removing belongings they feared might have been damaged or contaminated, in an effort to make the house habitable again and resume their daily lives.

But the family’s return was not without anxiety, particularly for al-Natsha’s four-year-old daughter, Ilya. Her biggest concern was the fate of her pet bird, “Natosh”, which she had left inside the house when the family was forced to leave.

Al-Natsha has no idea where the bird is, whether it is dead, or whether the Israeli soldiers released it. Ilya, meanwhile, keeps asking about her pet.

The return of families to al-Jalada came after 10 days of military restrictions and evacuations affecting several neighbourhoods in Hebron.

During the operation, hundreds of families were forced to leave their homes, while shops and institutions in the areas were closed.

According to previously released figures from the Hebron Governorate’s Support and Relief Committee, 537 families, comprising approximately 3,300 people, were displaced.

With residents now returning, the extent of the damage to homes and belongings, and the lasting effects of the days spent away, remain part of the experience of families trying to rebuild their lives.

For 68-year-old Khaled Shawer, who also lives in the neighbourhood, the damage to homes and the debris and destruction left behind by the military operation could be dealt with. What mattered most was that residents had returned and could begin to regain a sense of stability.

“Everything can be replaced: the destruction, the damage, the dirt, everything,” Shawer said. “But the most important thing is that we have returned to our homes, our paradise on Earth, the place where we find our psychological and physical stability.”
